title: Making a course book with Quarto
text:
Welcome
This is a short, practical guide for teachers at Utrecht University who want to turn a course reader into a website — one that students can search, read on a phone, and click through, with live simulations sitting next to the text.
We use Quarto and RStudio. Quarto itself is only a publishing framework: it works just as happily from Jupyter notebooks or VS Code, and with Python or Julia instead of R. We describe the RStudio route because, within the Biology department, that is the environment most colleagues already have open.

title: Making a course book with Quarto
text:
What you end up with
Two books in our own department are built exactly this way, and everything in this guide is drawn from their source:

Biologische Modellen en Statistiek — a full Dutch-language course book with interactive statistics applets, shared LaTeX macros, and a printable PDF from the same source.
Modeling Life — an English course website with embedded simulations and mini-projects.

Between them they run to hundreds of pages, and neither required anyone to learn web development.

title: Making a course book with Quarto
text:
How to read this






TipIn a hurry?



Read 2  Setting up in RStudio, press Render, and come back for the rest when you need it.








ImportantOne extension needed



9  Code students can run in the browser contains two live R cells that students can edit and run in the browser, so the book needs the quarto-live extension. It travels with the project in _extensions/, so a copy of this folder needs nothing installed.
If you ever see “Include directive failed” or an error naming readExtensionFormat, that folder is missing — Installing it has the one command that fetches it, and the two edits that switch live cells back off.



Getting started — installing things, making the project, and the one configuration file that decides everything.
Writing — text, maths, code that runs, callouts, exercises, figures, and getting a decent PDF out of the same source.
Interactive material — embedding simulations, code your students can edit and run in the browser, and self-contained applets. This is the part that makes a Quarto book worth the effort.
Building and publishing — rendering fast, putting it online for free, and what to check when something breaks.

title: Making a course book with Quarto
section: This book is also the starter book
text:
This book is also the starter book
You do not have to start from an empty folder. This book is itself the starter book — every chapter is a working demonstration of the thing it describes, so copying it hands you the UU house style, a working _quarto.yml, a live applet, a real figure, and an example of every pattern you are likely to need.
Download the starter book (.zip) — then see Option A: start from this book for how to open it in RStudio.

title: 1  What Quarto is, and why bother
text:
1.1 Why it suits teaching
Quarto is a free, open-source publishing system. You write in plain text — .qmd files, which are Markdown plus optional live code — and Quarto renders that same source into a website, a book, a PDF, slides, or a Word document.
If you have used R Markdown, this is its successor: the same idea, grown up and no longer tied to R.
Everything is text. Your book is a folder of readable files. It fits in Git, it diffs sensibly, and a colleague can open it in any editor.
Maths renders properly. LaTeX between dollar signs, in the browser and on paper, from one source.
Code can run. A plot in your reader can be generated by the code that produced it, so the figure and the analysis never drift apart.
Simulations sit next to the explanation. A student can read the model and then immediately turn its knobs — see Chapter 8. And with Chapter 9 they can edit your R or Python and run it, in the browser, with nothing installed. This is the part that really pays off.
Structure comes free. Sidebar, search box, chapter numbering, cross-references and a table of contents are all generated for you.

title: 1  What Quarto is, and why bother
text:
1.2 What you need to install
Three things, in this order.

R — the language.
RStudio Desktop — the editor. RStudio v2022.07 and later has built-in Quarto support.
Quarto — the publishing system.

Recent RStudio versions ship with a copy of Quarto bundled, so step 3 is sometimes optional. Install it separately anyway: it means you know which version you have, and can say so to a colleague.
Restart RStudio after installing Quarto so it notices.






NoteWhich version am I on?



In RStudio: Tools → Terminal → New Terminal, then type quarto --version. This is the only time in this guide you need a terminal, and you can skip it if you would rather not.



RStudio’s About screen showing the bundled Quarto version, and a terminal showing quarto --version.

title: 1  What Quarto is, and why bother
text:
1.3 Document, website, or book?
One file — _quarto.yml at the top of your folder — decides what you are building.








type:
What you get
Good for




default
A single standalone document
A hand-out, a practical, one lecture


website
Many pages with a top navigation bar
A course site: schedule, links, materials


book
Numbered chapters, a sidebar, cross-references, and a combined PDF
A course reader



A book is a website with extra structure, so starting as a website and graduating to a book later costs almost nothing. This guide assumes a book.
crumbs: 1  What Quarto is, and why bother

title: 1  What Quarto is, and why bother
text:
1.4 Not an R user?
Almost nothing here is really about R. Write ```{python} instead of ```{r} and your code chunks run Python; Julia and Observable JS work too, and a book can mix them. If your book is entirely Python, set engine: jupyter in _quarto.yml.
Everything else — the structure, the figures, the callouts, the iframes, the publishing — is identical whichever language you use, and identical whether you edit in RStudio, VS Code, Positron or a plain text editor.
crumbs: 1  What Quarto is, and why bother

title: 2  Setting up in RStudio
text:
2.1 Option A: start from this book
Ten minutes, once. At the end you will have a real book rendering in front of you.
There are two ways in, and the second is usually the better one.
The book you are reading is itself the starter book. Every chapter is a worked demonstration of the thing it describes — the figures in Chapter 5 are real figures, the applet in Chapter 8 really runs, the maths in Chapter 6 really renders. Copy the folder and you inherit all of it: the UU house style, a working _quarto.yml, a sensible .gitignore, and an example of each pattern you are likely to need.
Download the starter book (.zip)
Then:

title: 2  Setting up in RStudio
text:
TipOpening a downloaded folder in RStudio




Unzip it somewhere sensible and rename the folder to your course.
In RStudio: File → New Project… → Existing Directory → browse to that folder → Create Project.
Existing Directory is the option people miss, because the wizard’s first screen pushes you towards New Directory. It creates nothing of its own — it tells RStudio “this folder is a project”, writes an .Rproj file into it, and opens it. Everything already in the folder stays exactly as it is. (The zip deliberately contains no .Rproj, so the one RStudio makes will be named after your folder.)
Press Render. You should get this book back, running locally — nothing else needs installing.
Now start replacing. Open _quarto.yml, change the title and author, and work through the chapters one at a time: keep the scaffolding, delete our prose, write yours.









NoteWhat to keep, what to throw away



Keep: _quarto.yml (edit it), uu.scss, .gitignore, README.md, the figures/ and applets/ folders, and applets/AI-prompt-template.md. Keep make-starter-zip.R only if you want to hand your book on the same way.
Throw away once you no longer need them: our chapter files, and every ::: {.screenshot} block — those are our drafting markers, and Section 3.4 explains how they are styled. Search the project for {.screenshot} to find them all.

title: 2  Setting up in RStudio
text:
2.2 Option B: start from nothing
If you would rather see a book grow from an empty folder, RStudio will make you one.

title: 2  Setting up in RStudio
text:
2.3 Make the project
File → New Project… → New Directory → Quarto Book.
Give the folder a name. Tick Create a git repository if you already know you want to publish it (see Chapter 12) — it is easier to tick now than to add later. Press Create.
RStudio opens the new project, and you are already looking at a working book.

RStudio’s New Project → Quarto Book dialog, and the resulting folder in the Files pane.

title: 2  Setting up in RStudio
text:
2.4 Press Render
The Render button sits in the toolbar above the editor. The first render takes a minute; the finished book then appears in RStudio’s Viewer pane, and as files in a folder called _book (or docs — see Chapter 3).

title: 2  Setting up in RStudio
text:
2.5 Turn on Render on Save
The tick-box next to the Render button. Now every save refreshes the preview by itself.
This is the single change that makes writing a book pleasant rather than laborious. Do it before you write anything.

The Render button in the toolbar with Render on Save ticked, and the preview pane updating after a save.

title: 2  Setting up in RStudio
text:
2.6 Source or Visual?
Top-right of the editor pane there is a Source / Visual toggle.
Visual gives you a Word-like view — real bold text, real tables, menus for inserting figures, equations and cross-references — while still saving a plain text file underneath. A colleague who does not want to see any markup at all can live here permanently.
Source shows the markup. It is faster once you know it, and it is what the rest of this guide shows.
Most people end up switching back and forth: Visual for tables and equations, Source for everything else.






TipTables are the killer feature of Visual mode



Markdown tables are miserable to write by hand and trivial in Visual mode. Insert one there, then switch back to Source.

title: 2  Setting up in RStudio
text:
2.7 What is in the folder







Item
What it is




_quarto.yml
The book definition: which chapters, in which order, with which theme. The only file you truly must understand — see Chapter 3.


index.qmd
The front page.


*.qmd
One file per chapter. This is where you write.


_book/ or docs/
The finished website. Generated — never edit anything in here, it is overwritten on every render.


*.Rproj
RStudio’s project file. Double-click it to reopen the book later.


_freeze/
Stored results of code that has already run — see Chapter 11.









ImportantNever edit the output folder



_book/ and docs/ are built from your .qmd files. Anything you type in there disappears at the next render. If you find yourself editing HTML, you are in the wrong folder.

title: 3  The control panel: _quarto.yml
text:
3.1 A minimal book
This one file is the table of contents, the theme, and the settings. Get comfortable here and the rest of Quarto is just writing.
Three blocks matter:

title: 3  The control panel: _quarto.yml
text:
project:
  type: book
  output-dir: docs          # where the finished website is written

book:
  title: "My Course Book"
  author: "Your Name, Utrecht University"
  chapters:
    - index.qmd             # the front page
    - part: "Getting started"     # groups chapters under a heading
      chapters:
        - 01-writing.qmd
        - 02-figures.qmd
    - part: "Practicals"
      chapters:
        - 03-practical.qmd
  appendices:               # lettered instead of numbered
    - answers.qmd

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo            # any Bootswatch theme
    toc: true
  pdf:
    documentclass: scrreprt # delete if you never want a PDF


project — what you are building, and where the output goes.
book — the structure, and which chapters in which order.
format — how each output type looks.







ImportantThe mistake everyone makes once



A chapter that is not listed under chapters: does not exist. Creating week3.qmd is not enough — Quarto will render the book without it and give you no warning at all. If a chapter is missing from the website, this is why, nine times out of ten.



_quarto.yml open in the editor with the project / book / format blocks highlighted, next to the rendered sidebar, so the mapping is obvious.

title: 3  The control panel: _quarto.yml
text:
3.2 Controlling the sidebar labels
A long chapter title makes an ugly sidebar entry. Give the sidebar its own shorter text:
    chapters:
      - text: "Introduction"
        href: Modellen/intro_modellen.qmd
Chapters can live in subfolders, as this example shows. Paths in _quarto.yml are relative to the top of the project.

title: 3  The control panel: _quarto.yml
text:
3.3 Indentation
YAML indentation is meaningful, and must be spaces, never tabs. If Quarto complains about the file and the message makes no sense, an indentation slip is almost always the cause. RStudio inserts spaces for you if you leave its defaults alone.

title: 3  The control panel: _quarto.yml
section: 3.4 Making it look like Utrecht University
text:
3.4 Making it look like Utrecht University
Start from a Bootswatch theme — cosmo, flatly and litera all read well as a textbook — and layer your own SCSS on top:
format:
  html:
    theme: [cosmo, uu.scss]
That is what this book uses, and the single entry is deliberate. Quarto will happily give you a light/dark pair with a toggle in the corner:
    theme:
      light: [cosmo, uu.scss]
      dark:  [darkly, uu-dark.scss]
The theme listed first is the default, and the reader’s choice is remembered in their browser. Add respect-user-color-scheme: true and it follows their operating system instead.






NoteWhy this book has no dark mode



The UU identity is specified on a white ground: red and yellow are defined against paper, and yellow in particular becomes a different colour entirely on a dark surface. A dark palette would be something we invented, not something the university sanctioned — so this book stays light for every reader. Your own book can decide differently; the mechanism is right there above.


An SCSS file has two blocks. The defaults block sets variables before Bootstrap is compiled; the rules block is ordinary CSS applied afterwards.
/*-- scss:defaults --*/
$uu-yellow: #FFCD00;    // UU geel — our most distinctive colour
$uu-red:    #C00A35;    // UU rood
$primary:   $uu-red !default;
$font-family-sans-serif: "Open Sans", Arial, sans-serif !default;
$headings-font-family:   "Merriweather", Georgia, serif !default;
$font-size-root: 17px !default;

/*-- scss:rules --*/
h2 { border-bottom: 2px solid $uu-yellow; }

The UU standard fonts are Merriweather and Open Sans (with Zilla Slab permitted for headlines). All three are on Google Fonts, so a book can use them directly. Link them in the page header:
format:

    include-in-header:

TipSteal this book’s theme



uu.scss in this project is a complete, commented UU house-style theme — the palette, the fonts, callouts mapped onto the supporting colours, and the yellow accent rules. Copy that one file plus the theme: and include-in-header: blocks from this book’s _quarto.yml into yours, and you are done.
There is a starting point for a dark variant in _archive/uu-dark.scss if you decide your book wants one.








CautionA note on using yellow





UU yellow is a signature colour but a poor text colour — it fails contrast requirements on white. Use it the way the university does: as an accent rule, an underline, a highlight, a block of background. Keep body text and links in red, black or dark blue.




The same chapter side by side in light and dark mode, and the uu.scss file showing the $primary colour change.

  favicon: figures/favicon.png

  sidebar:
    logo: figures/uu-logo.png

The official UU logo files are on the corporate identity site; download the right variant rather than taking one off a web page.

title: 4  Writing a chapter
text:
4.1 Text and headings
A .qmd file is Markdown — plain text with a few marks for emphasis — plus three Quarto additions: maths, runnable code, and cross-references.
**bold**, *italic*, `code`, [link](url). A blank line starts a new paragraph.
One # is the chapter title, ## a section, ### a subsection. The ## headings are what fill the table of contents on the right of every page, so they are worth naming well.
Add {.unnumbered} after a heading to keep a page out of the chapter numbering — useful for a preface, a schedule, or a links page.

title: 4  Writing a chapter
text:
4.2 Maths
Inline between single dollars: $N_{t+1} = \lambda N_t$ gives \(N_{t+1} = \lambda N_t\). Displayed between double dollars, with a label so you can point at it later:
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}N}{\mathrm{d}t} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)
$$ {#eq-logistic}
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}N}{\mathrm{d}t} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)
\tag{4.1}\]
Writing @eq-logistic anywhere in the book now produces a numbered, clickable reference: Equation 4.1.
Chapter 6 is a full reference for the notation — symbols, multi-line equations, statistics, and how to define your own shorthand once and use it in both the website and the PDF.

title: 4  Writing a chapter
text:
4.3 Code that runs
A chunk marked {r} is executed when you render, and its output lands on the page.

t <- 0:40
logistic <- function(r, K = 100, N0 = 2) {
  N <- numeric(length(t)); N[1] <- N0
  for (i in 2:length(t)) N[i] <- N[i-1] + r * N[i-1] * (1 - N[i-1]/K)
  N
}
plot(t, logistic(0.10), type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 110),
     xlab = "time", ylab = "N")
lines(t, logistic(0.20), lwd = 2, lty = 2)
lines(t, logistic(0.35), lwd = 2, lty = 3)
legend("bottomright", c("r = 0.10", "r = 0.20", "r = 0.35"), lty = 1:3, lwd = 2)







Figure 4.1: Logistic growth for three values of \(r\).





Because that chunk carries label: fig-growth, it is referenceable as Figure 4.1.
Chunk options go one per line at the top of the chunk, each starting with #|:



Table 4.1: Chunk options you will actually use.





Option
Effect




echo: false
run the code, hide it from students


eval: false
show the code, don’t run it


code-fold: true
hide the code behind a “Show the code” toggle


code-summary: "..."
the text on that toggle


warning: false
suppress R’s warnings


label: fig-…
make the output referenceable as a figure


fig-width, fig-height
size in inches












TipSet the defaults once



Options that should apply everywhere belong in _quarto.yml:
execute:
  echo: true
  warning: false
Individual chunks can still override them.

title: 4  Writing a chapter
text:
4.4 Code that is only shown
To display code without running it — Python that students will run themselves, for instance — use a plain fenced block with no curly braces: write ```python rather than ```{python}. You still get syntax highlighting, and nothing executes.

title: 4  Writing a chapter
text:
4.5 Callouts
Five kinds, and they are the workhorse of a teaching book.






Note



note — background information, an aside.








TipA title



tip — advice. A ## heading on the first line becomes the callout’s title.








Important



important — the thing students must not miss.








Warning



warning — a common mistake.








CautionClick to see the answer





caution — and with collapse="true" it starts folded shut. This is how you put a hint or a worked answer right next to the question without giving it away.



::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Click to see the answer
Hidden until the student expands it.
:::

title: 4  Writing a chapter
text:
4.6 Exercises that number themselves

Exercise 4.1 (Carrying capacity) Using Equation 4.1, what happens to \(\mathrm{d}N/\mathrm{d}t\) when \(N = K\)?

Write down the answer.
Check it against Figure 4.1.


::: {#exr-carrying}
## Carrying capacity
Using @eq-logistic, what happens when $N = K$?
:::
Refer to it as @exr-carrying → Exercise 4.1. Reorder your chapters and every number in the book renumbers itself.

title: 5  Figures and tables
text:
5.1 Inserting a figure
Put the image in a figures/ folder next to your chapters, and write one line:
The text in square brackets is the caption. ![]() with an empty caption is allowed, but a caption is nearly always worth writing — it is the part students read first.

title: 5  Figures and tables
text:
![A caption students will actually read.](figures/example-figure.svg)



Two ways of coping with biological complexity: simplify it into a model, or measure it and use statistics.

title: 5  Figures and tables
text:
5.2 Sizing, alignment and labels
Options go in curly braces after the image:
![Caption](figures/example-figure.svg){#fig-example width=55% fig-align="center"}






Figure 5.1: The same figure at 55% width, centred.



width is best given as a percentage so it adapts to the reader’s screen. fig-align takes left, center or right. The #fig- id makes it Figure 5.1.






Important{#example} does nothing; {#fig-example} works



See Table 4.2. The prefix is what tells Quarto it is looking at a figure.

title: 5  Figures and tables
text:
5.3 Which file format



Table 5.1: Choosing an image format.










For
Use
Because




Diagrams, schematics, anything you drew
SVG or PDF
stays sharp at any zoom, tiny file


Photographs, microscopy
JPG
small files for continuous tone


Screenshots, exported plots
PNG
sharp edges, no compression smear






Keep images under about 500 kB. A 3 MB photograph makes the page slow for a student on a phone, and if the book is in Git it stays in the repository forever.

title: 6  Maths and LaTeX
text:
6.1 Inline and displayed
Quarto writes maths with LaTeX notation. You do not need to learn LaTeX — you are not typesetting a document with it, only writing formulas — but a page of the notation goes a very long way in a biology course book.
The same source is rendered twice: by MathJax in the browser and by LaTeX itself in the PDF. You write it once.
Inline maths sits between single dollars, inside a sentence:
The population grows at rate \(r\) until it approaches \(K\).
Displayed maths sits between double dollars, on its own lines, and is centred:
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}N}{\mathrm{d}t} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)
\]

title: 6  Maths and LaTeX
text:
The population grows at rate $r$ until it approaches $K$.


$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}N}{\mathrm{d}t} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)
$$







ImportantLeave the dollars tight against the maths



$r$ works. $ r $ may not — Quarto uses the spacing to tell maths from an ordinary dollar sign. If you need a literal dollar in your text, escape it: \$.

\(x_1, \ldots, x_n\)






Greek letters are their names with a backslash: $\alpha \beta \gamma \delta \lambda \mu \sigma \tau \phi \theta \rho$ gives \(\alpha \beta \gamma \delta \lambda \mu \sigma \tau \phi \theta \rho\). Capitalise the first letter for the capital form: $\Delta$, $\Sigma$, $\Omega$ gives \(\Delta\), \(\Sigma\), \(\Omega\).

title: 6  Maths and LaTeX
text:
6.3 Statistics notation



Table 6.3: Notation for the statistics chapters.










You want
You write
You get




sample mean
$\bar{x}$
\(\bar{x}\)


estimate
$\hat{\beta}$
\(\hat{\beta}\)


expectation
$\mathbb{E}[X]$
\(\mathbb{E}[X]\)


variance / sd
$\mathrm{Var}(X)$, $\mathrm{SD}(X)$
\(\mathrm{Var}(X)\)


probability
$P(X > x)$
\(P(X > x)\)


conditional
$P(A \mid B)$
\(P(A \mid B)\)


distributed as
$X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$
\(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\)


null hypothesis
$H_0: \mu = \mu_0$
\(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\)


degrees of freedom
$t_{n-1}$
\(t_{n-1}\)












TipUse \mid, not |, for “given”



A bare | in $P(A|B)$ is typeset as an ordinary bar with no spacing. \mid is the real conditional-probability symbol and gets the spacing right.

title: 6  Maths and LaTeX
text:
6.4 Words inside formulas
Anything you type in maths mode is set in italic, letter by letter, as if every character were a variable. That is wrong for words and for units:
Wrong:  $rate = births - deaths$
Right:  $\text{rate} = \text{births} - \text{deaths}$
Wrong: \(rate = births - deaths\)
Right: \(\text{rate} = \text{births} - \text{deaths}\)
Use \text{...} for words, and \mathrm{...} for upright single symbols such as the d in a derivative — \mathrm{d}N, not dN.

title: 6  Maths and LaTeX
text:
6.5 Multi-line equations
Two environments cover almost everything. aligned lines equations up on a chosen character — put an & where the alignment should happen and \\ at the end of each line:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t} &= aR - bRC \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}C}{\mathrm{d}t} &= cRC - dC
\end{aligned}
$$
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t} &= aR - bRC \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}C}{\mathrm{d}t} &= cRC - dC
\end{aligned}
\]
cases is for a piecewise definition:
$$
f(x) =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } x < 0 \\
1 & \text{if } x \geq 0
\end{cases}
$$
\[
f(x) =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } x < 0 \\
1 & \text{if } x \geq 0
\end{cases}
\]
A matrix, if you need one:
$$
J = \begin{pmatrix}
\partial f / \partial x & \partial f / \partial y \\
\partial g / \partial x & \partial g / \partial y
\end{pmatrix}
$$
\[
J = \begin{pmatrix}
\partial f / \partial x & \partial f / \partial y \\
\partial g / \partial x & \partial g / \partial y
\end{pmatrix}
\]
pmatrix gives round brackets, bmatrix square ones, vmatrix the vertical bars of a determinant.

title: 6  Maths and LaTeX
text:
6.6 Brackets that grow
Ordinary brackets stay small and look wrong around a tall fraction. Prefix them with \left and \right and they scale:
Small:  $(1 - \frac{N}{K})$
Grown:  $\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)$
Small: \((1 - \frac{N}{K})\)    Grown: \(\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)\)
\left and \right must come in pairs. If you want only one visible bracket, pair it with \right. (a full stop means “nothing here”).

title: 6  Maths and LaTeX
section: 6.7 Numbering and referring to an equation
text:
6.7 Numbering and referring to an equation
Put a #eq- label after the closing $$:
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}N}{\mathrm{d}t} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)
$$ {#eq-logistic2}
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}N}{\mathrm{d}t} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)
\tag{6.1}\]
Then @eq-logistic2 gives Equation 6.1, numbered and clickable, and the numbering fixes itself when you reorder chapters. For a custom label, [see @eq-logistic2] gives see 6.1.






NoteThe label goes outside the dollars



$$ ... $$ {#eq-name} — on the same line as the closing $$. Inside the maths it is just more maths, and Quarto will not see it.

title: 6  Maths and LaTeX
6  Maths and LaTeX
text:
6.9 Where MathJax and LaTeX disagree
They agree on almost everything, and then they do not. Watch for:

Packages. \usepackage{amsmath} and friends only exist in the PDF. MathJax has most of amsmath built in, so the common environments work anyway — but an exotic package will render on paper and silently fail on the web.
\text{} needs no package in either. Prefer it to \mbox{}.
Coloured maths. \color{red}{...} works in MathJax; in the PDF it needs \usepackage{xcolor} in _macros.tex.
Line breaks. \\ inside aligned is fine in both. A bare \\ in inline maths is not — put multi-line maths in a display block.
Unicode. Typing α directly usually works in HTML and breaks the PDF. Write \alpha.







ImportantAlways look at both outputs before a course starts



Render to HTML and PDF and skim the equations in each. A formula that silently fails in one output is the single most common way a course book embarrasses itself.

title: 6  Maths and LaTeX
text:
6.10 When something does not render
A formula that shows as raw \frac{...} text, or a chunk of the page that has gone blank, is nearly always one of these:



Table 6.4: Maths that will not render.









Symptom
Cause




Raw LaTeX visible on the page
Unbalanced $ or $$ somewhere earlier in the chapter


Everything after a point is italic
An unclosed $


\left error
A \left with no matching \right


Works in HTML, breaks in PDF
A missing \usepackage, or a Unicode character


Works in PDF, breaks in HTML
A LaTeX package MathJax does not implement


Nothing renders in one chapter
A missing {{< include _macros.tex >}} line












TipTwo tools worth knowing



Detexify lets you draw a symbol and tells you its LaTeX name. And RStudio’s Visual editor has an equation editor with a live preview — insert the equation there, then switch back to Source to see what it wrote.

title: 7  Getting it onto paper
text:
7.1 Two different splits, and they are not the same thing
A course book usually has to exist as a PDF as well as a website, and students will print pages from the browser whether or not you planned for it. Both are handled from the same source — with care.
This trips up everyone once, so here it is before anything else. There are two mechanisms, and they answer different questions.
A book that produces a PDF and expects students to print pages needs both. The BMS book uses content-visible 33 times and the CSS classes 35 times — for different jobs.

title: 7  Getting it onto paper
text:
content-visible when-format
.screen-only / .print-only




Asks
Which output is Quarto building?
Is the browser painting to screen or paper?


Resolved
Once, at render time
In the reader’s browser, every time they print


Splits
HTML file vs PDF file
The same HTML page, on screen vs printed


Use for
A PDF edition of the book
A student pressing Ctrl-P on a web page

title: 7  Getting it onto paper
section: 7.2 Content that only exists in one format

title: 7  Getting it onto paper
7  Getting it onto paper
section: 7.4 A real PDF, rather than printing a web page
text:
7.4 A real PDF, rather than printing a web page
Printing from the browser is always a compromise. If the PDF matters, add a proper format:
format:
  html:
    theme: [cosmo, uu.scss]
  pdf:
    documentclass: scrreprt
    include-in-header: _macros.tex
Rendering then produces both. This needs a LaTeX installation; if you have none, quarto install tinytex sets up a small self-contained one.






TipLaTeX feels like too much?



format: typst is a modern, much lighter alternative that needs no LaTeX toolchain at all. It does not yet do everything LaTeX does — check your maths and your cross-references carefully — but for a straightforward reader it is fast and pleasant.

title: 8  Embedding interactive content
text:
8.1 The pattern
An iframe is a whole webpage shown inside a box on your page. It is the single most useful trick in a course book, because it lets a student turn a knob instead of reading about the knob. The BMS book does it about fifty times.
There are two flavours, written almost identically:
External — you point at a page on someone else’s server: Desmos, YouTube, JSFiddle, a simulation on tbb.bio.uu.nl.
Internal — you point at an HTML file that lives inside your own project. Nothing external is involved and it keeps working forever.
Raw HTML must be wrapped in a {=html} block, or Quarto escapes it and students see the angle brackets:
width="100%" makes it responsive to the page width. height is fixed per embed and has to suit the content — the BMS book uses anything from 330 to 680 px. The inline style (no border, rounded corners, a little vertical margin) is what makes an embedded tool look like part of the page rather than a box someone dropped in.

title: 8  Embedding interactive content
8  Embedding interactive content
section: 8.2 External: a simulation on another server
text:
8.2 External: a simulation on another server





Simulation: rabbits in Australia. The interactive version is at https://tbb.bio.uu.nl/bvd/simulations/australia/

<iframe src="https://tbb.bio.uu.nl/bvd/simulations/australia/"
        width="100%" height="520" title="Rabbits in Australia"
        style="border:none; border-radius:8px;"></iframe>

title: 8  Embedding interactive content
text:
8.3 External: a Desmos graph
Build the graph on desmos.com/calculator, press Share, and use the URL you are given — https://www.desmos.com/calculator/qxycdqwsdq — directly as the src. Students can then drag its sliders inside your book. The maths chapters of the BMS book use thirteen of these.
<iframe src="https://www.desmos.com/calculator/qxycdqwsdq"
        width="100%" height="467"
        style="border:1px solid #ccc;" frameborder="0"></iframe>

title: 8  Embedding interactive content
8  Embedding interactive content
section: 8.5 External: code students can edit and run
text:
8.5 External: code students can edit and run
JSFiddle hosts a small program together with its output. Append /embedded/result to the share URL for output only, or /embedded/js,result to show the code beside it so students can change a parameter and press Run.
<iframe src="https://jsfiddle.net/bramvandijk88/jq3u7f6t/embedded/result"
        width="100%" height="550" title="Simulation"></iframe>






WarningExternal things break



Every external iframe is a promise made by somebody else. Servers move, accounts lapse, embedding gets blocked — and you find out when a student emails you in week 4. Check them at the start of each course year, and for anything students are assessed on, make it internal.

title: 8  Embedding interactive content
section: 8.6 Internal: an applet inside your own book
text:
8.6 Internal: an applet inside your own book
One self-contained .html file in a folder in your project. The src is then just a relative path:
```{=html}
<iframe src="applets/example-applet.html"
        width="100%" height="620"
        title="Logistic growth explorer"
        style="border:none; border-radius:8px; margin:1em 0;">
</iframe>
```
Which gives you this — a real applet, running inside this page:





Applet: logistic growth explorer. Sliders for \(r\), \(K\) and \(N_0\), with the resulting trajectory. Open the book in a browser to use it.

Notice that both examples on this page are wrapped in ::: {.screen-only}, with a ::: {.print-only} block beside them. That is not decoration — it is the whole print story, and Section 7.3 explains why.
That is the entire mechanism. The statistics chapters of the BMS book work exactly this way: Statistiek/Applets/ holds a critical-value calculator, a p-value calculator and a sampling-distribution simulator, each one file. Nothing external, nothing that can go offline, and the applets travel with the book.






ImportantFour things that go wrong



Blank box. The path is wrong. It is relative to the chapter file, so a chapter in a subfolder needs ../applets/….
It vanishes after rendering. Add resources: [applets/] to _quarto.yml so Quarto copies the folder into the finished site.
The box is too short and the applet gets its own scrollbar. Iframes never grow to fit their contents — tune height by hand, then check on a phone.
A stray quote. height=600" — missing its opening quote — silently breaks the whole tag. There is one of these in the BMS book right now (Statistiek/ToetsenGemiddelde.qmd). If an applet renders strangely, check the quotes before anything else.



The rendered page above, showing the applet embedded in the text — this is the image that sells the whole approach to a colleague.

title: 9  Code students can run in the browser
text:
9.1 What it looks like
This is the newest of the interactive options, and for a course that teaches programming it is the most useful. The student edits your code and presses Run, and it executes in their browser — no R installed, no server, no accounts, no logins that break in week 3.
Both cells below are real. Each is an editor with Run Code and Start Over buttons: change anything, run it again, and reset it when you have made a mess.
Small on purpose: the very first cell on a page has to download R itself, so a three-line example gets the student to their first Run Code quickly. Once webR is loaded, everything else on the page is instant.
The second cell is a real model — change d to 0.9 and the paracetamol takes far longer to clear:
crumbs: 9  Code students can run in the browser

title: 9  Code students can run in the browser
text:
NoteThese two are live



Press Run Code. The first cell has to fetch R itself, so give it a few seconds; after that everything on the page is instant. Section 9.3 explains how this was set up, and how to switch it back off.
crumbs: 9  Code students can run in the browser

title: 9  Code students can run in the browser
section: 9.2 Where this sits among the other options
text:
9.2 Where this sits among the other options



Table 9.1: The three kinds of interactive content.











Option
Who wrote the code
Can the student change it?
Where does it run




External iframe (Chapter 8)
Someone else

Internal applet (Chapter 10)

The student’s browser

An applet is the right choice when you want a student to explore a relationship. A runnable code cell is right when you want them to write the code.
crumbs: 9  Code students can run in the browser

title: 9  Code students can run in the browser
text:
9.3 Installing it
The extension is Quarto Live, and installing it is the one moment in this guide that needs a terminal. It is one command, run once per project.






TipStep by step, in RStudio




Open the project (File → Open Project, or double-click its .Rproj).
Click the Terminal tab — bottom-left pane, next to Console.
Check where you are. Type pwd and press Enter. It must print your project folder. If it prints your home folder instead, move there first:

cd ~/Dropbox/…/YourBookFolder

Now install:

quarto add r-wasm/quarto-live

It asks whether you trust the authors — press Y, Enter. It may ask a second time to confirm; Y again.
Check it worked: a folder _extensions/r-wasm/live/ should now exist in the project. In RStudio’s Files pane you may need the More → Show Hidden Files option to see it.









WarningThe mistake that costs ten minutes



quarto add installs into whatever folder the Terminal is currently in, not into the project you have open in RStudio. Those are usually the same thing, but not always — a Terminal that opened in your home folder will cheerfully create _extensions there, report success, and leave your book exactly as broken as before.
That is what step 3 is for. If it has already happened, just drag the stray _extensions folder into your project.


Commit the _extensions/ folder to Git along with everything else. Then a colleague who clones the book does not have to install anything, and neither does a build server.
crumbs: 9  Code students can run in the browser

title: 9  Code students can run in the browser
text:
9.4 Switching the book over
Two edits, both one line.
In _quarto.yml, change the html format to live-html:
format:
  live-html:          # was: html
    theme: [cosmo, uu.scss]
    toc: true
live-html is ordinary html with the WebAssembly machinery added, so everything else — the theme, the sidebar, cross-references — carries on unchanged.
At the top of every chapter that has a live cell, immediately below the closing --- of the YAML header:
{{< include ./_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}
That line registers webr as an engine that knitr recognises, and it is needed whenever your book runs R chunks anywhere — which it almost certainly does. Miss it and Quarto stops with “Include directive failed”; miss the live-html change and the cells render as ordinary dead code blocks with no Run button. This chapter has both — look at its source.






NoteGoing back



Reverse the same two edits: live-html back to html, delete the include line, and put engine: markdown in the chapter header so Quarto stops looking for something to execute. The book then renders on any machine with no extension installed, which is what you want before handing it to a colleague who has not installed anything.
crumbs: 9  Code students can run in the browser

title: 9  Code students can run in the browser
text:
9.5 Writing a cell
A live R cell is a {webr} block. That is the whole syntax — you write this:
```{webr}
plot(sin(seq(0, 4 * pi, 0.1)), type = 'l', lwd = 2, col = "#C00A35")
```
…and your students get this:








Source above, result below — the same three backticks either way. Every example from here on is shown in that pair.
crumbs: 9  Code students can run in the browser

title: 9  Code students can run in the browser
text:
9.6 Cell options
Options go at the top of the cell, #| style, exactly like ordinary chunks — the cell above uses caption and min-lines.



Table 9.2: Live cell options.









Option
Effect




autorun: true
run once as the page loads, so the student sees output before touching anything


edit: false
show and run it, but do not let them change it


runbutton: false
no Run button — pair with autorun for a live demo


startover: false
remove the reset button


persist: true
remember the student’s edits in their browser across reloads


min-lines, max-lines
control the height of the editor box


timelimit: 10
seconds before a runaway loop is stopped (default 30)


caption: "Try changing d"
a title on the cell


include: false
run it invisibly — for setup code the student should not see






Options change the cell quite a lot. This one is set to run itself on page load and refuse edits — a live demonstration rather than an exercise:
```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| caption: Exponentiële versus logistische groei
```








Notice there is no Run button and no editor — it simply appeared. Compare it with the cells at the top of the chapter, which have both.






WarningLive cells need a web server — and Render alone does not start one



Open docs/index.html straight off your disk and the cells appear but stay dead: the editor never initialises, because browsers refuse to start the WebAssembly worker over a file:// address. It looks exactly like a broken install, and it is not.
Render builds the book but does not necessarily serve it. Worse, once the format is live-html RStudio no longer recognises it as something it knows how to preview, so the Render button quietly stops opening a preview window at all — it prints “Output created: docs/index.html” and nothing appears.
To see live cells locally, start a server yourself. In the Terminal tab, from the project folder:
quarto preview
That builds the book, serves it at a http://localhost:#### address, opens your browser at it, and re-renders whenever you save. Stop it with Ctrl+C.
If it opens inside RStudio’s Viewer pane rather than a real browser, click the Show in new window icon — the Viewer is a cut-down browser and WebAssembly is exactly the sort of thing it is bad at.
Published to GitHub Pages the book is served over https://, so students never meet any of this.








TipThe setup-cell pattern



Put data loading and library calls in an include: false cell at the top of the chapter. State carries between cells on the same page, so the student’s cell can then be three lines about the actual idea instead of fifteen lines of boilerplate.
crumbs: 9  Code students can run in the browser

title: 9  Code students can run in the browser
text:
9.7 Packages
Packages must be declared in the YAML so they are fetched when the page loads:
webr:
  packages:
    - dplyr
    - ggplot2






WarningNot every package exists in WebAssembly



An R package has to have been compiled for WebAssembly. Most of the common ones are, at repo.r-wasm.org, and R-universe builds WebAssembly versions automatically — add a repos: key to pull from one. But anything wrapping compiled C or Fortran that nobody has ported will simply not be there.
Check the packages you need before you rewrite a practical around this. Python has the same limitation, with a different list — see Section 9.8. Every live cell in this chapter uses only base R or the Python standard library, deliberately.
crumbs: 9  Code students can run in the browser

title: 9  Code students can run in the browser
text:
9.8 The same trick for Python
There is nothing to install. The extension you already added ships Pyodide — CPython compiled to WebAssembly — alongside webR, and the include line at the top of this chapter registers both engines. Write {pyodide} instead of {webr} and it simply works:
```{pyodide}
#| caption: Exponentiële groei
r, N = 0.12, 2.0
for t in range(10):
    print(f"t = {t:2d}   N = {N:6.2f}")
    N = N * (1 + r)
```
Which gives you a Python editor, with its own Run Code button:








Packages work the same way, under their own key:
webr:
  packages: [dplyr, ggplot2]
pyodide:
  packages: [numpy, matplotlib]
Pyodide ships the scientific stack, and micropip can fetch pure-Python wheels from PyPI — but not packages whose compiled parts have never been built for WebAssembly. Same caveat as R, different list.






WarningOne page, two runtimes



This page now loads both webR and Pyodide, because it has cells of both kinds. That is roughly double the first-load cost, and this chapter only does it to show you that it works.
In a real course book, keep a page to one language unless you genuinely need both. Where you do — an introductory course where half the room knows R and half knows Python — a ::: {.panel-tabset} with an R cell in one tab and a Python cell in the other is the tidy way to do it.
crumbs: 9  Code students can run in the browser

title: 9  Code students can run in the browser
text:
9.9 What it costs






ImportantThe first cell on a page is slow



Loading webR means downloading R itself — tens of megabytes. Expect a few seconds on a good connection and rather longer on eduroam in a full lecture hall. After that it is fast, and it is cached for the rest of the session.
Two things help: put an autorun: true cell early on so the download starts while the student is still reading, and do not scatter live cells across twenty chapters when three practical pages would do.


Two more limits worth knowing before you commit a practical to this:

No files and no network. The browser sandbox means no reading from the student’s disk and no download.file(). Ship data inside the page, or as a URL the extension is configured to fetch.
It is not a replacement for teaching them to install R. If the course outcome is “can run an analysis on their own laptop”, they still have to install it. This is for the explaining, not for the doing.
crumbs: 9  Code students can run in the browser

title: 9  Code students can run in the browser
section: 9.10 Does it work in the PDF?
text:
9.10 Does it work in the PDF?
No — like everything else in this part of the book, a live cell needs a browser. Wrap it the way Chapter 7 describes: the live version inside ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}, and for the PDF a plain non-executing code block showing the same code, so the printed book still has something to read.
crumbs: 9  Code students can run in the browser

title: 9  Code students can run in the browser
text:
9.11 Writing about live cells
There is a trap here, and this chapter walks into it deliberately so you do not have to.
Quarto picks an engine per file by scanning the raw text for cell fences, before it parses any markdown. A ```{webr} fence therefore counts even when you only meant to show it as an example — nesting it inside a bigger code block, indenting it, or adding backticks makes no difference. In a book with no live cells at all, that alone is enough to make Quarto demand a Python kernel and stop with:
Starting python3 kernel...
Jupyter is not available in this Python installation.
The syntax examples on this page are therefore written as raw HTML blocks rather than fenced ones — look at the source. They still get a copy button, Quarto never sees a fence at all, and it is what lets this chapter print a cell’s source and run that same cell directly underneath.






TipIf you only want to describe live cells



A chapter that shows the syntax but runs nothing needs neither the extension nor the include. Put engine: markdown in its YAML header and Quarto will stop looking for something to execute.
crumbs: 9  Code students can run in the browser

title: 10  Writing applets with an AI assistant
text:
10.1 Constrain the request
A single self-contained HTML file with a few sliders and a plot is exactly the kind of thing Claude or ChatGPT produces well in one go. This is where the effort really collapses: the statistics applets in the BMS book are of this kind, and each took minutes rather than days.
The catch is in the title of this chapter’s key section: if you are careful.
The constraints below are what separate a file that still works in five years from one that mysteriously stops working in March.
crumbs: 10  Writing applets with an AI assistant

title: 10  Writing applets with an AI assistant
text:
One single .html file. All CSS and JavaScript inline. No npm, no build step, no separate files. If the answer needs installing, it is the wrong answer.
No external libraries, no CDN links. Plain JavaScript and a <canvas> element cover almost everything a statistics or modelling applet needs. A library pulled from a CDN means the applet dies whenever that CDN does, or whenever a student has no connection.
Say the width is fluid and give the height. “It will be embedded in an iframe at width: 100%, height: 620px. Use a responsive layout; nothing may overflow at that height.”
Ask it to set the background colour explicitly, and to handle light and dark colour schemes. Otherwise the applet inherits nothing and looks unfinished.
Ask it to state the formula it implemented in a comment at the top of the file, in mathematical notation. That one line is what makes the file checkable.







CautionA prompt you can paste






Write me a small interactive teaching applet as one single, self-contained HTML file.
Topic: [what it should show — e.g. “the sampling distribution of the mean: the student sets the population SD and the sample size n, draws many samples, and sees the distribution of sample means beside the population distribution”]
Controls: [which sliders or inputs, and their ranges]
Language of all labels: [English / Dutch]
Hard requirements:

One file. All CSS and JavaScript inline. No npm, no build step.
No external libraries and no CDN links. Plain JavaScript and <canvas> for plotting. It must work with no internet connection.
It will be embedded in an iframe at width: 100%, height: [N]px. Use a responsive layout; nothing may overflow or scroll inside the frame.
Set the background colour explicitly on body, and support both light and dark via prefers-color-scheme.
Readable at phone width.
Put a comment at the very top stating exactly which formula or algorithm you implemented, in mathematical notation.
Keep it simple and readable — I need to be able to check it.

Start with the simplest version that works. I will ask for additions afterwards.
crumbs: 10  Writing applets with an AI assistant

title: 10  Writing applets with an AI assistant
text:
10.2 Then check it






ImportantAn applet that looks convincing and computes the wrong thing is worse than no applet



Students trust it more than they trust you. Five minutes, every time.



Read the formula comment at the top of the file. Is it the formula you actually teach, in your notation?
Open the file directly in a browser by double-clicking it, before any iframe is involved. It must work standalone.
Check three numbers against R. Pick inputs you can compute yourself, including one extreme case. For a p-value applet: does it agree with 2 * pt(-abs(t), df = n - 1)?
Push every slider to both ends. \(n = 1\), \(\alpha = 0\), \(r\) at maximum. AI-written applets are reliably right in the middle of the range and reliably produce NaN, an empty plot or a freeze at the edges.
Check the language and notation match the rest of your book. Assistants drift into English and into whatever notation is commonest online.
Narrow the browser window to phone width.
Render the book and open the real chapter page, not just the file.







NoteThis is not hypothetical



The applet embedded in Chapter 8 was written this way and then run through the list above. Steps 3 and 4 caught a real bug: at very low growth rates it labelled a population that was still slowly growing as “oscillating”, because the classifier only looked at the spread of the last few values and never asked whether they were still rising. Correct everywhere in the middle of the range, wrong at the edge — exactly the failure mode step 4 exists to catch.
crumbs: 10  Writing applets with an AI assistant

title: 10  Writing applets with an AI assistant
text:
10.3 The rhythm that works
Ask for the smallest version first — one slider, one plot — and check it. Then ask for one addition at a time.
A 500-line applet produced in a single shot is genuinely hard to verify. The same applet grown over four steps is easy, because you checked each step while it was still small.
crumbs: 10  Writing applets with an AI assistant

title: 10  Writing applets with an AI assistant
section: 10.4 If you do accept a CDN link
text:
10.4 If you do accept a CDN link
Sometimes a plotting library is worth it. The BMS applets use Chart.js this way. If you go there:

Pin the exact version — chart.js@4.4.0, never chart.js@latest.
Know that you have made your book depend on somebody else’s server, and that the applet will not work offline or in an exported copy.
Note it somewhere, so whoever inherits the book knows why it broke.
crumbs: 10  Writing applets with an AI assistant

title: 11  Rendering, and keeping it fast
text:
11.1 Two buttons, two commands
Render builds the whole project into _book/ (or docs/). In RStudio it is the toolbar button; from a terminal it is quarto render.
Preview starts a live server that re-renders on save and refreshes the browser. In RStudio this is what Render on Save gives you; from a terminal it is quarto preview.
You can work entirely from the buttons for an ordinary book. Two exceptions where you need quarto preview in the Terminal instead:
quarto preview builds, serves at http://localhost:####, opens a browser, and re-renders on save. Ctrl+C stops it.
crumbs: 11  Rendering, and keeping it fast

title: 11  Rendering, and keeping it fast
text:
Anything that needs a real web server — live webR cells (Chapter 9) are dead over a file:// address.
Any custom format, live-html included. RStudio only auto-previews formats it knows, so Render prints “Output created” and no window appears.
crumbs: 11  Rendering, and keeping it fast

title: 11  Rendering, and keeping it fast
text:
11.2 freeze and cache
Both stop Quarto re-running code unnecessarily. They solve different problems and live in different places, and the distinction is worth teaching clearly because the names do not help.






Notefreeze — file level, about portability



With freeze: auto, Quarto runs a chapter’s code once, stores the results in a _freeze/ folder, and reuses them until that .qmd changes.
Commit _freeze/ to Git and the payoff is large: a colleague — or a build server — can render the whole book without having R and every package installed, because the computed results travel with the repository.
freeze: true never re-runs. freeze: false always runs fresh.








Notecache — chunk level, about speed while writing



cache: true uses knitr’s cache to skip re-running an individual chunk whose code has not changed, so a slow simulation does not re-run on every preview. The caches live in per-chapter *_cache/ folders.


Rule of thumb: cache for “this chunk is slow while I am writing”, freeze for “someone else should be able to build this without my setup”. They combine, and both can be overridden per file or per chunk.
execute:
  freeze: auto
  cache: false






WarningCached results can go stale



Both mechanisms trust the source text, not the world. If a chunk reads a data file and the file changes but the code does not, you will keep the old result. Delete _freeze/ and *_cache/ and re-render when you have changed anything a chunk depends on but does not contain.
crumbs: 11  Rendering, and keeping it fast

title: 11  Rendering, and keeping it fast
section: 11.3 What actually makes a book slow
text:
11.3 What actually makes a book slow
In practice, in this order:

Code that runs on every render. Fix with freeze: auto.
A LaTeX PDF build. Fix by only rendering the PDF when you need it: Render → Render Book → HTML only, or quarto render --to html.
Huge images. See Chapter 5 — keep them under about 500 kB.







TipRender one chapter while drafting



quarto preview 08-iframes.qmd renders just that file. In RStudio, pressing Render while a single .qmd is open does the same thing. Cross-references to other chapters will not resolve in that preview — that is expected, and they come back in a full render.



The Render button and its dropdown showing the format choice, and the live preview refreshing after a save.
crumbs: 11  Rendering, and keeping it fast

title: 12  Putting it online
text:
12.1 Three routes
Once it renders, your book is just a folder of static files. Any web server can host it — including a free one.
The rest of this chapter is the GitHub Pages route, done without ever opening a terminal.

title: 12  Putting it online
text:
Route
Effort
Good for




GitHub Pages
Set up once, then Commit + Push
A course book you will keep editing. Free, versioned, and a colleague can contribute.


A UU server
Ask your local support to host the folder
Something that must live under a uu.nl address. The BMS book is served this way.


Quarto Pub
One command
A quick demo or a one-off hand-out.

title: 12  Putting it online
text:
12.2 The idea
Your book folder becomes a repository — a folder that GitHub keeps a copy of. You render the website into a subfolder called docs, send it to GitHub, and tell GitHub to serve that folder as a website.

title: 12  Putting it online
text:
12.3 Step by step
1. Point Quarto at docs. In _quarto.yml:
project:
  type: book
  output-dir: docs
Render once. The finished website now appears in docs/.
2. Add a file called .nojekyll. An empty file, at the top of your book folder. In RStudio: File → New File → Text File, then save it with exactly that name, leading dot included. It stops GitHub from reprocessing your site and quietly mangling parts of it.
3. Make the folder a repository. If you did not tick “Create a git repository” when making the project: Tools → Project Options → Git/SVN → set version control to Git, and restart RStudio. A Git tab appears next to Environment and History.
4. Create the repository on GitHub and connect it. Make a free account, press New repository, give it a name, leave it empty. GitHub then offers you a list of terminal commands — to avoid those, install GitHub Desktop, choose Add existing repository, point it at your book folder, and press Publish repository.
5. Send your work up. From then on, in RStudio’s Git tab or in GitHub Desktop: tick the changed files, write a one-line message saying what you changed, press Commit, then Push. Those three actions are the whole of Git for this purpose.
6. Switch the website on. On github.com, in your repository: Settings → Pages → under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch, choose your main branch, and set the folder to /docs. Save.
A minute later your book is live at https://<your-username>.github.io/<repository-name>/.






TipFrom then on



Write. Render. Commit. Push. The website updates itself within a minute or two. There is nothing else to remember.



GitHub’s Settings → Pages screen with Source set to the main branch and /docs, and the resulting live URL in a browser.

title: 12  Putting it online
text:
12.4 Before you make it public






WarningA GitHub Pages site is visible to anyone with the address



And so is everything else in the repository — including files you never listed in _quarto.yml, because the source is published too.
Keep exam questions, model answers you do not want found, and anything with student data out of the book folder entirely. Not merely unlisted: out. Answer chapters that are meant to be public are fine; the danger is the file you forgot was in there.


A .gitignore file keeps generated and personal files out of the repository. A sensible starting point:
.Rproj.user/
.Rhistory
.RData
.DS_Store

/.quarto/
_book/
**/*.quarto_ipynb
**/*_cache/

*.aux
*.log
*.toc
Note that _freeze/ is deliberately not ignored — see Chapter 11.

title: 12  Putting it online
section: 12.5 Working on a book with a colleague
text:
12.5 Working on a book with a colleague
Two people editing different chapters is easy. Two people editing the same paragraph is a conflict, and no tool prevents that — agree who owns which chapters for a given course block.
One rule removes most of the pain: pull before you start, push when you stop. A week of uncommitted edits is what turns a small overlap into a large one.






ImportantEveryone must use the same Quarto version



Different Quarto versions produce different HTML from identical source. If two people render the same book with different versions and both commit the output, every push rewrites the entire site and every merge becomes a conflict.
Agree a version, write it down in the repository, and check it with quarto --version when someone new joins.

title: 13  When it breaks
text:
13.1 Reading an error message
Almost everything that goes wrong in a Quarto book is on this list.
Quarto’s errors usually name the file and the line. Two habits help:

title: 13  When it breaks
text:
Render one chapter at a time when hunting a problem. A full book render buries the useful line in a hundred others.
Look above the red text. The actual cause is often the last thing Quarto said it was doing successfully, not the line where it finally gave up.

title: 13  When it breaks
text:
13.2 Where to look next

The official Quarto documentation is genuinely good and searchable. The authoring section covers layout, callouts and cross-references; the books section covers structure.
The fastest way to learn a trick is still to open a book you like and read the .qmd that produced the page. Both departmental books are readable source: Onderwijs/BMS/Boek and Onderwijs/Modeling_Life/Course_Website.
There is a copyable starter book at Onderwijs/Quarto Books/starter-book.







TipAsk an assistant, but give it the file



Claude and ChatGPT know Quarto well. Paste the actual _quarto.yml and the actual error message rather than describing them — most Quarto problems are one wrong character, and it will spot it faster than you will.

title: About this guide
text:
Source material
Written for teachers at Utrecht University who want to turn a course reader into a website.
It merges three sources:
The theme follows the Utrecht University corporate identity: Merriweather and Open Sans as the standard fonts, UU red for links, UU yellow as the accent, and the supporting palette for callouts. uu.scss in this project is free to copy into your own book.
The book is deliberately single-theme: the UU palette is defined against white paper, so there is no dark mode and no toggle. See Making it look like Utrecht University if you want one anyway.
